newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asia Metals - Japan aluminium premiums at US$87-$88.
newsitem.headline: Asia Metals - Japan aluminium premiums at US$87-$88.

text.p: Japan third quarter aluminium supply contract premiums over London Metal Exchange (LME) cash prices have mostly been raised to a base of US$87-$88 a tonne CIF from $82 in the second quarter, dealers said on Friday.

"Premiums will be at $87-$88 for the third quarter. I believe that the talks on the premiums for the most important Japanese companies have already been concluded and that will probably be the range," one dealer.
Traders believe most Japanese companies will have concluded negotiations by next week because the premium for spot business is prohibitive.
The premium for spot aluminium deliveries in Japan was averaging recently between $95-$97 a tonne CIF.
"You'll have to pay a considerably higher amount if you want spot delivery," a dealer said.
Robust demand for aluminium has fuelled the strong rise in premiums and dealers discounted reports in Japan that consumption will soon ease.

"It's a tactic. Some of the negotiations are still going on. My answer to that would be: 'Then why are you buying aluminium in these quantities?' Demand is still going very strong," one industry official said.
Another dealer said the strong growth of aluminium demand can also be seen in relatively small markets such as Malaysia and the Philippines.

Third quarter supply premiums in both nations were averaging at around $95-$100 a tonne CIF for Malaysian ports and Manila, dealers said. The level for Indonesia was also set at $95-$100 a tonne CIF Jakarta.
"Nobody will sell to Indonesia below $95," a trader said.
In Taiwan, third quarter premiums were set at $90-$95 a tonne CIF Kaohsiung and Keelung. Korean premiums were pegged at $90-$95 a tonne CIF Pusan.
Premiums for Hong Kong, which also serves the China market, were set at $95-$100 a tonne CIF.

With economic growth rates across the region expanding at a steady pace, traders said they see aluminium consumption increasing at a healthy level for key consumers like the car, can and construction sectors.
"Everyday, there is demand coming in. Business here is really going very well," an aluminium trader said.

The strenth of consumption can be seen in the sharp fall of aluminium stocks on LME, dealers said. Aluminium stocks on Thursday reached 744,650 tonnes, down 95,200 tonnes from the level around the middle of April.
A dip in underlying aluminium prices may also stimulate consumer buying in the region, dealers said.
LME brokers Brandeis said three-month aluminium closed poorly on Thursday, finishing at $1,622 a tonne.
"A triple top appears to be forming which does not bode well for prices. Next support is seen at $1,607/10 (a tonne)."
In another development, zinc traders forecast that more metal may be placed on warrant at the LME's Singapore warehouse if the price of the metal climbs to $1,370 a tonne.
Three-month zinc was seen by the trade at 1,652/57 a tonne at 0400 GMT against a close in London of $1,357.
"At $1,370, I think they'll place most of the stuff on warrant. If it does not go to that level, they'll probably wait for maturity which is probably in the June date," a dealer said.
Zinc stocks at the LME warehouse here reached 18,050 tonnes on Thursday, a rise of 6,800 tonnes from the start of the week. Most of the material is believed to have come from China.
"I think 10,000 tonnes remains off-warrant," a zinc dealer said. "I did not hear of any new cargo coming in."
